title: Samarkand R10 (open): Uzbekistan enter final round with one-point lead over India
summary:
Five teams with chances to grab gold

Uzbekistan will enter the final round of the Chess Olympiad with a one-point lead after producing one of their most convincing performances of the tournament. The hosts defeated Armenia 3½–½ on Saturday, while India kept up the pressure with a victory by the same score against Uzbekistan 2.

With one round remaining, Uzbekistan lead on 18/20 match points, India follow on 17/20, while Germany, Ukraine and Hungary all stand on 16/20. Those are the five teams that still retain a chance of finishing first in Samarkand.

The final round will bring confrontations involving the contenders. Uzbekistan will face Ukraine, giving the latter a chance to catch the leaders on match points with a match victory. India will meet Hungary, while Germany take on the Netherlands. The Dutch belong to an eight-team group on 15/20 and are no longer in contention for first place.

The decisive round will begin four hours earlier than usual, at 8.00 CEST.

Round 11 pairings

Eastern Time

...103 boards

Nodirbek Abdusattorov, Javokhir Sindarov and Nodirbek Yakubboev were all part of the team that won the 2022 Chess Olympiad in Chennai | Photo: Rafal Oleksiewicz / FIDE

Uzbekistan make short work of unbeaten Armenia

Armenia had been one of the most resilient teams in the tournament before meeting the hosts. Through nine rounds, they had lost only two individual games, and both defeats had merely cost them a single match point in draws against higher-seeded United States and Netherlands.

Uzbekistan, however, broke through much more decisively.

Javokhir Sindarov and Mukhiddin Madaminov scored relatively quick victories after their Armenian opponents went wrong tactically in double-edged middlegames. Nodirbek Abdusattorov then added a third win, although his game against Haik Martirosyan required considerably more patience, as Abdusattorov eventually converted an endgame with rooks and opposite-coloured bishops.

The final 3½–½ score was particularly notable given how difficult Armenia had been to beat throughout the event.

A remarkable team leader, on and off the board - 22-year-old Nodirbek Abdusattorov | Photo: Rafal Oleksiewicz / FIDE

Uzbekistan's success has been built on strength across all four boards. Abdusattorov, the only member of the team to have played all ten rounds, has scored 8/10 and leads all board-one players with a 2900 tournament performance rating.

Sindarov and Yakubboev are also near the top of the individual standings. Sindarov currently sits second among board-two players, behind Jorden van Foreest of the Netherlands, while Yakubboev is second on board three behind Germany's Frederik Svane.

After nine match victories in ten rounds, Uzbekistan now need one final strong result to complete their campaign on home soil.

Javokhir Sindarov and Mukhiddin Madaminov, who both won on Saturday, are also good friends and successful collaborators | Photo: Rafal Oleksiewicz / FIDE

India remain within one point

India were facing a very different type of challenge against Uzbekistan 2. On three of the four boards, the defending champions enjoyed rating advantages of more than 200 Elo points - itself an indication of how strongly Uzbekistan's second team had over-performed to reach the top tables in round ten.

The rating gap eventually showed in the result. Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu, Nihal Sarin and Gukesh Dommaraju all won, while Arjun Erigaisi drew Abdimalik Abdisalimov to complete a 3½–½ victory.

Once again, Gukesh made an important contribution. The world champion has now scored 8½/10 and, like Abdusattorov, has played in every round. His 2797 tournament performance rating makes him the clear favourite for individual gold on board four.

His form has also been particularly valuable in the closing stages. In round nine, Gukesh had been the player who decided India's match against Germany, defeating Alexander Donchenko in the only decisive game of a 2½–1½ victory.

India will now finish against Hungary, knowing that anything less than a win would make it extremely difficult to overhaul Uzbekistan.

Gukesh Dommaraju is having a great run in Samarkand | Photo: Michal Walusza / FIDE

Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu remains undefeated on board one, with 6/9 points to his name | Photo: Michal Walusza / FIDE

Ukraine earn their first major upset

Ukraine kept their title chances alive with their most important result of the event so far, beating fourth-seeded China 3–1. It was Ukraine's first upset match victory of the Olympiad, and it came at exactly the right moment.

Igor Kovalenko defeated Ding Liren on board one, while 18-year-old European champion Roman Dehtiarov beat Kong Xiangrui on board four. The other two games ended drawn, with Vasyl Ivanchuk holding Wei Yi and Ihor Samunenkov sharing the point with Xu Xiangyu.

Samunenkov has been Ukraine's most consistent individual performer. The 17-year-old has scored 7½/9 on board four and currently sits second in the individual rankings on that board, behind only Gukesh.

Igor Kovalenko defeated none other than former world champion Ding Liren on the top board | Photo: Michal Walusza / FIDE

Roman Dehtiarov converting his advantage against Kong Xiangrui as captain Alexander Beliavsky follows the action closely | Photo: Michal Walusza / FIDE

Svane brothers deliver once again

Germany also remained in the race by defeating France 3–1, and the pattern of the match was by now a familiar one.

Vincent Keymer and Matthias Bluebaum drew on the top two boards, while Frederik and Rasmus Svane supplied the wins on boards three and four. The same script had already worked for Germany against Türkiye and, more importantly, against Uzbekistan earlier in the tournament. The two brothers have repeatedly provided the decisive points when Germany have needed them.

Frederik Svane, in particular, has had an outstanding event. He leads the individual standings on board three with 8/10 and a 2819 tournament performance rating.

Germany's final opponents will be the Netherlands, who defeated Romania 2½–1½ in round ten thanks to Jorden van Foreest's victory on board two.

With the Svane brothers as team heroes, Germany beat France to remain in contention for overall victory | Photo: Rafal Oleksiewicz / FIDE

Hungary stay in contention

Hungary are the fifth team still mathematically capable of taking first place after defeating Spain 3–1. Their match was quite different from Germany's, as all four games ended decisively. Richard Rapport, Peter Leko and Gleb Dudin scored the Hungarian wins, while Jaime Santos Latasa defeated Benjamin Gledura for Spain.

Dudin, who entered the tournament as Hungary's reserve, has become one of the team's most reliable scorers. He now has 7/9 and enters the final round on a run of four consecutive victories. That form could be important against India, with both teams needing a win to maximise their chances at the top.

Behind the five title contenders, eight teams stand on 15/20: the United States, Azerbaijan, Türkiye, Croatia, Uzbekistan 2, the Netherlands, Armenia and Serbia.

Living legend Peter Leko scored a crucial win on Saturday | Photo: Michal Walusza

The duel of prodigies between 15-year-old Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus and 12-year-old Faustino Oro favoured the Turkish rising star, who obtained a 28-move win to help Türkiye defeat Argentina by a 3-1 score | Photo: Michal Walusza /FIDE

title: Interview with the Olympic winners from Uzbekistan: "We have many more victories to come!"
summary:
Nobody came close!

The Uzbekistan Open team has done it again! After stunning the chess world by winning the Olympiad in 2022, they are champions once again, this time on home soil at the 46 th FIDE Chess Olympiad!

Uzbekistan took gold with 20 match points and 32½ game points | Source: ChessBase Olympiad portal

We caught up with the gold medal-winning team after the closing ceremony to relive the key moments, the pressure of playing at home, and the team spirit behind the title.

Interview by Sagar Shah

Sagar Shah: Congratulations, guys, you have won the gold! In 2022, we had an interview. Four years later, you guys are champions again, this time in Uzbekistan. How are you feeling?

Sindarov: We feel fantastic. Very happy to win the Olympic gold medal in our country. We are very proud to become champions in our home country, where everyone supports us.

Raw moments from Samarkand as Uzbekistan wins the Chess Olympiad 2026 | Video: ChessBase India

Sagar: You have won a beautiful trophy. I want to start this interview with your game, Javokhir, the queen sacrifice (against Diego Saul Rodri from Peru). I think it was very beautiful: 31...Kf7 and then 32...Rh3. What a game!

Sindarov sacrificed his queen by playing 31...Kf7! Can you find the reason behind the move?

Sindarov: The game was interesting, but in the end, you know, it was just a choice. Any other move was around nine or ten moves long, but 31...Kf7 was just making some aura. I was thinking during the game that maybe I shouldn't play this move, but in the end I decided, okay, come on, let's play for some videos, for some content, real stuff. But it's an easy move. I won't say it's something crazy.

Sagar: Nodirbek, you have two gold medals. You were incredible on board one, like a machine. You didn't lose a game. You won game after game. Brilliant play!

Nodirbek played all the rounds and didn't lose a single game! | Source: Chess results

Nodirbek: I am extremely happy to be part of this incredible team. These guys are simply the best on their boards, and in chess in general. They all belong in the top ten. They play at a very high level. I am lucky to have such strong teammates, and I am proud to be here with the boys, with everyone. I did my job on the first board. I played very safe at times and won some games as well. I worked very hard before this tournament, so I wouldn't let the team down, and I am very happy that I succeeded.

Not a single loss he faced! | Photo: Michal Walusza

Sagar: Yakubboev, you were the guy who won so many critical games. Against Türkiye, you scored the win. Against India, you scored the win again.

Yakubboev: This time I had this role, let's say: winning important games. But the other teammates also performed very well. It wasn't planned. It wasn't a planned situation. Somehow I finished last, and I somehow managed to win. But I am happy to get a point for our team. This time I had this role. (Smiles)

Yakubboev in demand! | Photo: Michal Walusza

Sagar: Tell us about your game with Nihal, this 39...Nxh4, this 39.gxh4+ Nxh4. What a moment that was. Maybe the most important moment of the Olympiad, would you say?

A terrible blunder by Nihal, 37...Nf5? , which made him lose his queen. Can you find out how?

Yakubboev: I think so, because the match against India was the most important for us. It decided the whole standings. After that match, we could really fight for a medal. If we had lost that match, I don't think we would have tried to win this medal. It was important. And he missed that 38.Ne6+ check. I saw it earlier, when he took on g5. I saw ...Kg7, which is a winning move. When he took on g5, I felt a bit happy. Then I played 37.g3 , and it was already a complicated game. I was not worse; I was in the game. ...Kg7 was the decisive moment for our team.

Nodirbek: He wasn't the only one who was happy after 36...Kg5 . We were all watching his game like crazy. We went crazy after 38...Ne6+. Our chat was screaming.

Sagar: Were you doing live commentary, or were you just watching privately?

Sindarov: On Lichess.

A crucial victory for Uzbekistan as they defeated India in round six | Photo: Michal Walusza

Sagar: Shamsiddin, you played 11...b5 against Gukesh in the opening. I think it was an incredible hold with the black pieces, and a very important game. You gave him no chance.

Shamsiddin: Yeah, I know the lines. It was preparation. I saw it one or two months ago, not on the preparation day. I just remembered it. I know that after b5 it's easy to equalise. We are all happy to have won. We won all the important matches: USA, India and China. We are all happy.

Sagar: Mukhiddin, I have to tell you, the last round you played so good. And you had another victory yesterday. That was just insane. How did you find those amazing moves like 29.d5 and 30.h5?

Mukhiddin: In general, I am very happy. I didn't feel a lot of pressure on this team, since I have a very strong team, as you can see. I just tried to play simple chess, and if I got a chance, I tried to use it. Yesterday, when I was playing against Gabriel Sargissian, I felt after the opening that my position was slightly better, so I started to push.

Black played 27...Qb7? . Can you find a better move?

At some point it was close to equal, but then he missed it and blundered with 27...Qb7 . I played 28.Bb5 . I felt that 28...Nd8 was very bad. I pushed 29.d5 , and after he took on d5, I played 30.h5 . I felt that his king was in trouble, so that's why I went for it.

Sagar: Amazing. Nodirbek, Javokhir spoke about this aura moment. I think you playing 1.e4 d5 was one such aura moment. There's a nice reel where you played it, everyone smiled, and then you smiled too.

Nodirbek: Yeah. I told them about twenty minutes before the game that I would play d5, and everyone went crazy. At first they didn't believe I would play it, and then when they saw...

Yakubboev: But we discussed it in the team meeting.

Nodirbek: Yeah, we discussed it briefly in the team meeting. I had some options, like ...c5, the Caro-Kann or the Scandinavian, but I said I would decide myself. In preparation, I saw that he has no practice at all in the Scandinavian, so I tried it against him, and it worked. The whole idea was inspired by Arjun, as I said. He played it in the last round in Budapest and won a nice game, so I also tried to steal his aura.

Sagar: And Javokhir, you played Nf3 and b3 (against Robert Hovhannisyan from Armenia) with such good preparation. I think you were prepared until around move 20.

Javokhir: Yeah, but because of that good preparation, it was just equal in the end. But my opponent somehow played a really bad game in this match. I got lucky. He started giving me his first and second pawns; I captured all of them, and I won a game I didn't expect to win. I was really shocked by how my opponent played. Robert is generally a very solid player, but in this game he somehow played really badly, which surprised me. But it was good preparation. Sometimes you need to be lucky to win this tournament.

Sagar: Today, against Ivanchuk, was also a tough game.

Javokir: Yeah, a very tough game.

Sagar: At one point you thought for 40 minutes and played 14...Na5.

Javokhir: Yeah, I was trying to remember the line because I had seen it somewhere before the tournament. I was checking that line because I had played some blitz games here. Then somehow I forgot it, and I tried to remember the best equalising move, but I couldn't. It was a very unhappy moment. I tried to remember for 40 minutes, but I didn't find it. I played a move of my own, and it really wasn't a good one. Then he got some advantage, but I managed to draw, which made the team happy, and we won. When I draw, I understand that we will win the match easily.

Prime Minister of Uzbekistan Abdulla Aripov visited the Chess Olympiad 2026 | Photo: Rafal Oleksiewicz

Sagar: Amazing. And guys, whenever you won, there was so much celebration. It was very heartwarming to see people care about chess so much. There were hugs, and so much energy. Was there pressure on all of you playing in your country? There were so many eyes on you. I think the Prime Minister of the country was also visiting, and he is also the president of the Uzbek Chess Federation. Was there pressure, or was it only "we have to do it"?

Mukhiddin: For me, the beginning of the tournament was very hard, as I said before. There was so much pressure on me in the first two rounds. But after that, I started playing, and my self-confidence got better. Then we believed in ourselves. And the match against India was important too. After that match, I think we really believed we were going to win.

Sagar: Amazing. Nodirbek, did you feel any pressure?

Nodirbek: I would say I felt a little pressure because we were playing in our own country. It's always a bit difficult. We also know how India played in Chennai. They were very close, but at some critical moments they made mistakes. They were nervous, and they couldn't win the whole thing. This time, I think we showed our absolute best. Everyone played amazing chess. We spent a lot of time together before the event, and I think we were in good physical shape and good form. We needed to prepare ourselves for that pressure and that environment, with a huge crowd watching our games every day and rooting for us. It was an unbelievable tournament, incomparable with any other event we have played so far. We are extremely happy that we managed to bring this trophy back to our country after Chennai. I think with this kind of team, we will have many more victories to come. Thank you.

Insane celebrations after Uzbekistan beat India | Video: ChessBase India

Sagar: Shamsiddin, you have each won 200,000 dollars, if I am not mistaken. I saw that. And the President has written such a beautiful message praising each one of you. He also wrote about Jakhongir. How does it feel?

Shamsiddin: I feel happy because our President supports chess. He takes care of us.

Each player of the gold medal Uzbekistan team gets US$200,000 from the Government of the country. The coach of the team gets US$50,000.

What is impressive is that the Government has chalked out the details for everything from winning the Olympiads to World Championships, Asian… pic.twitter.com/idxAbL0EaZ

— ChessBase India (@ChessbaseIndia) September 28, 2026

Sagar: Yakubboev, a few words about Rustam, the coach of the team. I think he was always there, even when you guys won. At one point you won, and he hugged you. I have never seen him with so many emotions.

Yakubboev: As I mentioned, he is our hero because we grew up watching his achievements and his games. If it weren't for him, maybe some of us wouldn't be playing chess. It's always nice to have your own captain, not one from another country. He is kind of your person, your man. He knows us very well. He knows our character, how we feel during the game, and how we think during the game. It was really nice to have him as our captain.

Rustam Kasimdzhanov: the captain behind the gold | Photo: Rafal Oleksiewicz

Captain proudly lifting the trophy! | Photo: Rafal Oleksiewicz

Yakubboev: I would also like to thank my other coaches. I have been working with Roman Vidonyak for more than a year. My second coach, I don't want to say his name. I am really happy to have him on my team.

Sagar: Is there anyone else you would like to thank? Any of you?

Sindarov: Many thanks to everyone's parents, Mr. President, Alisher Zafarovich Sa'dullayev. There are many people. My coach, Roman. My team members' coaches. Because of a lot of people, we became strong players. I want to thank all the fans who support us every day. Thanks to the government for organising this event. We enjoyed it. Of course, because we were playing in our home country, it was the best Olympiad we have played. We really loved it. Hopefully, with this team, I will try to play in other tournaments for gold medals.

title: Bodhana Sivanandan: Youngest-Ever WGM at 11
summary:
The English Chess Federation put its youngest player on top board for the Women's Olympiad in Samarkand: Bodhana Sivanandan, just 11 years old. This did not come as a complete surprise, as with her rating of 2354 (before the Olympiad), she was and remains England's number one female player, some way ahead of the experienced Jovanka Houska and Harriet Hunt, both of whom, however, are already somewhat past their peak.

Bodhana Siv anand an ( Notice anything? Surely that can't be a coincidence. And here too: Praggn anand haa.) repaid the faith placed in her with her performance. The 11-year-old played all eleven rounds and scored eight points on top board. After three wins, she drew against the strong Azerbaijani player Ulviyya Fataliyeva in round four and, for example, also held the world's top junior and reigning European Women's Champion Anastasiia Hnatyshyn to a draw. The experienced Nana Dzagnidze was also unable to get the better of Bodhana Sivanandan. The English player suffered just one defeat, in round eight against Peru's Deysi Cori.

With her performance, Bodhana Sivanandan finished 13th in the list of the best players on board one. She was the best player on her team and led England to 15th place in the final standings, five places higher than their starting rank based on average rating.

The result also earned her a WGM norm (Woman Grandmaster). It was Bodhana's third norm, meaning she has now fulfilled the requirements for the title. She is thus the youngest WGM in chess history, succeeding Kateryna Lagno, who received the title in 2002 at the age of twelve. Hou Yifan, later Women's World Champion, also received the title at the age of 12, in 2007. FIDE introduced the WGM title in 1976.

Bodhana's interest in chess began when a visitor to her parents' home left behind a chessboard at the start of the pandemic. Her father taught her the rules, and she improved her game with the help of YouTube tutorials. In 2021, she played her first tournament at the Harrow Chess Club. In 2022, at the age of seven, Bodhana won all 24 of her games at the European Schools Chess Championship. In the summer of 2026, she became the youngest British national champion of all time.

title: Wesley Sews Up First Titled Tuesday Of 2026
summary: GM Wesley So won Titled Tuesday on September 29, starting 7/7 on his way to a 9.5-point total. That score was enough for an outright victory after the top three boards in the final round, including his own, all ended in draws. One of the key figures of the upcoming Grandmasters documentary, So scored his first Titled Tuesday victory of the year, and fifth in just 75 attempts ever (a 6.7% win rate better than most 10-time winners). GM Denis Lazavik took second place with the top tiebreak in a seven-way tie on nine points. In case you missed it, here's this week's broadcast with GM Robert Hess: https://t.co/tRvPHraUOjThe Olympiad proved to be a useful warm up after all for the real event! @chesscom 😀🏆 🥇 🎉💪 So and Lazavik were among the 17 players to start 4/4, a list that did not include some usual suspects such as GM Hikaru Nakamura, who reached a Chess.com record 3470 blitz rating just before the event started, or last week's victor GM Alireza Firouzja, whose third-round win over GM Luca Moroni led Hess to the line of the week when he spotted the position after 21 moves: "I've never been more confused ever looking at a chess game... Can I resign for both players?" In the wild position, Moroni went for broke, but there was no mate to be found as Firouzja picked up a second queen and the win.

additionalSources.title: XTX London Chess Classic returns
additionalSources.summary:
Last year Uzbekistan's GM Nodirbek Abdusattorov produced a thrilling six-game winning streak on his way to an emphatic victory, a full two points clear of the chasing pack led by GM Alireza Firouzja. In doing so, Nodirbek finished just half a game point short of a performance rating of over 3,000, a feat only achieved four times in the history of chess.

This year's LCC features a huge range of events for players of all standards to enjoy:

The LCC Masters , an elite invitation-only all-play-all tournament featuring ten of the world's top grandmasters. We expect to be able to announce the line-up of the event soon.

The LCC Challengers , an invitation-only all-play-all tournament giving some of the best up-and-coming talents the chance to qualify for next year's LCC Masters.

The LCC Swiss , a 9-round classical tournament suitable for those seeking IM and GM norms.

A 5-round weekend classical tournament with rated sections: Open, U2000, U1750, U1500, U1250.

A 5-round weekday classical tournament with rated sections: Open, U1800, U1400

Evening blitz tournaments

The LCC team blitz tournament, for teams of four players.

The Pro-Biz Cup , an event that pairs our elite GMs with bidders from business and industry to raise funds for CSC.

The Super Rapid , a 10-round Swiss rapidplay event for everyone.

The LCC Dinner at the Dorchester Hotel, raising money to support the work of the charity.

Entries for all tournaments are now open on the LCC website . The 2026 XTX Markets London Chess Classic welcomes spectators who want to follow the action of our elite events. Visitors to London Novotel West will be able to watch the games in the playing hall or listen to live grandmaster analysis from our commentary team. Spectator tickets are available for Rounds 3 to 9 and can be purchased here .

Compete alongside the GMs in the Super Rapid

The 2026 XTX Markets London Chess Classic offers everyone the chance to compete against our elite GMs in the Super Rapid tournament. This two-day event held over the weekend of 5th/6th December will also feature some specially invited guests.

The format is a 10-round Swiss tournament held at London Novotel West. Can you rise to the top and take on some of the stars of world chess?

A special day out for schools

Each weekday, CSC will be welcoming 200 children from our Schools' Programme to the XTX Markets London Chess Classic. The children will enjoy a day of chess activities including:

lessons from a CSC tutor

simultaneous games against chess experts

the chance to meet and play a game against a Grandmaster

a tournament against their peers from around the country.

Invitations will be sent out by CSC's Regional Organisers soon and we hope to repeat the success of 2025 in welcoming schools from all over the country.

CSC Schools' Programme

While preparations for the 2026 XTX Markets London Chess Classic in November are now underway, our Schools' Programme has resumed in a record number of schools around the country. This term, CSC tutors will be delivering chess lessons and running chess clubs in over 450 schools nationwide.

To find out more about how CSC can support chess at your school, please visit the CSC website . We are particularly interested in hearing from members of staff who want to run their own chess clubs but need some assistance getting started. We have an amazing package of free equipment, training and support available for schools in which over 30% of the students receive free school meals.
